Move from base R and stringr

Source: vignettes/articles/from-base-r.Rmd
from-base-r.Rmd

This guide is for someone who already matches regular expressions with grepl(), sub() and regmatches(), or with stringr, and wants the zuregex call that does the same. It gives the equivalents in two tables, then shows the differences you would otherwise find by surprise.

library(zuregex)

The equivalent functions

Patterns that work in base R with perl = TRUE work unchanged: both use PCRE2. stringr matches with ICU, whose syntax is close but not the same, so check a pattern that uses anything beyond the common core.

Task Base R, perl = TRUE stringr zuregex
Does it match? grepl() str_detect() re_detect()
How many matches? lengths(gregexpr()) str_count() re_count()
Where is the first match? regexpr() str_locate() re_locate()
Where is every match? gregexpr() str_locate_all() re_locate_all()
The first match regmatches() with regexpr() str_extract() re_extract()
Every match regmatches() with gregexpr() str_extract_all() re_extract_all()
The groups of the first match regmatches() with regexec(), utils::strcapture() str_match() re_match()
The groups of every match gregexec() str_match_all() re_match_all()
Replace the first match sub() str_replace() re_replace(n = 1)
Replace every match gsub() str_replace_all() re_replace()
Split strsplit() str_split() re_split()
Quote metacharacters str_escape() re_escape()

Base R’s options become arguments that every re_*() function has.

Base R zuregex
perl = TRUE always on
ignore.case = TRUE flags = "i"
fixed = TRUE literal = TRUE
invert = TRUE re_detect(negate = TRUE)
useBytes = TRUE a raw vector, or strings marked as "bytes"

The subject comes first and the pattern second, as in stringr. With grepl() and sub() it is the other way round.

x <- c("2026-10-21 GET /index.html", "no date")
grepl("get", x, ignore.case = TRUE, perl = TRUE)
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE
re_detect(x, "get", flags = "i")
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE

Replacement replaces every match

re_replace() is gsub(), not sub(): it replaces all the matches unless n says otherwise. Compare the first two results, where only the year changes, with the third.

sub("\\d+", "#", x, perl = TRUE)
#> [1] "#-10-21 GET /index.html" "no date"
re_replace(x, "\\d+", "#", n = 1)
#> [1] "#-10-21 GET /index.html" "no date"
re_replace(x, "\\d+", "#")
#> [1] "#-#-# GET /index.html" "no date"

Templates use $, and know more

A replacement is a template in PCRE2’s syntax, where a group is $1 or ${name}. Base R writes \\1 and stops at nine groups, with no names. A base R template still works, since PCRE2 reads \\1 to \\9 as groups too.

sub("(\\d+)-(\\d+)", "\\2/\\1", x, perl = TRUE)
#> [1] "10/2026-21 GET /index.html" "no date"
re_replace(x, "(?<year>\\d+)-(?<month>\\d+)", "${month}/${year}", n = 1)
#> [1] "10/2026-21 GET /index.html" "no date"

A template can also give a default for a group that took no part in the match. The second version has no minor number, so ${2:-0} writes 0.

re_replace(c("v1.2", "v3"), "v(\\d+)(?:\\.(\\d+))?", "major $1, minor ${2:-0}")
#> [1] "major 1, minor 2" "major 3, minor 0"

?re_replace has the whole syntax, and replacement by a function.

No match is NA, not a missing element

regmatches() drops the elements that did not match, so its result is shorter than its input. re_extract() keeps one result per element.

regmatches(x, regexpr("\\d+", x, perl = TRUE))
#> [1] "2026"
re_extract(x, "\\d+")
#> [1] "2026" NA

Groups come back as a data frame

str_match() returns a character matrix whose first column is the whole match. re_match() returns a data frame of the groups only, named after them.

stringr::str_match(x, "(?<year>\\d+)-(?<month>\\d+)")
#>                year   month
#> [1,] "2026-10" "2026" "10" 
#> [2,] NA        NA     NA
re_match(x, "(?<year>\\d+)-(?<month>\\d+)")
#>   year month
#> 1 2026    10
#> 2 <NA>  <NA>

With proto it does the work of utils::strcapture(), and the two calls give the same typed data frame.

proto <- data.frame(year = 0L, month = 0L)
utils::strcapture("(\\d+)-(\\d+)", x, proto, perl = TRUE)
#>   year month
#> 1 2026    10
#> 2   NA    NA
re_match(x, "(\\d+)-(\\d+)", proto = proto)
#>   year month
#> 1 2026    10
#> 2   NA    NA

Patterns are never recycled

Base R uses only the first pattern of several, with a warning. zuregex follows stringr: a pattern has length one or the length of x. Anything else is an error, here three patterns for two strings.

re_detect(x, c("GET", "POST", "PUT"))
#> Error in `re_detect()`:
#> ! `pattern` must have length 1 or the length of `x` (2), not 3.

Splitting keeps a trailing empty piece

strsplit() drops an empty string after the last separator. re_split() keeps it, as Python’s re.split() and stringr::str_split() do.

strsplit("a,b,", ",", perl = TRUE)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "a" "b"
re_split("a,b,", ",")
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "a" "b" ""

See also

?re_detect describes the arguments every function shares. For the reasons behind these choices, read Design and motivation.
